title: The Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12; CCC 1716)
hookLine: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful

lines: A MAN SITS DOWN ON A HILL.
cards: Scroll through any feed and you'll see who the world calls blessed. The vacation in Greece, hashtag blessed. The new house, the promotion, the perfect family photo.
Now a man sits down on a hillside in Galilee, with farmers, fishermen and sick people around him, and starts a list of the blessed that sounds completely backwards. The poor. The ones who mourn.
The meek. The ones who get persecuted. It's the first thing he teaches in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and the Catholic Church calls it the heart of his preaching.

teach.b: Beatitude comes from the Latin beatus: blessed, happy. The Greek is makarios, the deep, lasting happiness of someone whose life is going right. So each line announces: this is where happiness is.
There are eight in Matthew, each with a promise. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." "Blessed are the meek: for they shall possess the land."
And: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." Then the ones who mourn, who hunger and thirst after justice, the clean of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted.

The Catechism says the Beatitudes are at the heart of Jesus's preaching, and that they paint a portrait of Jesus himself: the poor one, the meek one, the merciful one, the one who wept and was persecuted.
Read them again, and you're reading his face. Why do they matter? The Catechism says every human being has a desire for happiness written in them by God, and the Beatitudes answer it.
They don't say be poor and miserable. They say the happiness God offers isn't where the feed says it is: it's in an open hand, a gentle strength, a heart that forgives.
Jesus isn't handing out a new list of rules. He's describing the people God's kingdom belongs to, and inviting others to become like them.

how: The Beatitudes are read at Mass on the feast of All Saints and on several Sundays, and many Catholics use them to examine their conscience or pray one each day of the week.

o: blessings that say where true happiness lies
new commandments added to the old ten
attitudes a good believer ought to have

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: theirs is the kingdom of heaven

s: there are eight Beatitudes in Matthew's Gospel
the poor in spirit, the meek, those who mourn, the hungry for justice, the merciful, the clean of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted.
the Catechism says the Beatitudes paint a portrait of Jesus
he is the poor, meek, merciful one; reading them is reading his face.
the Beatitudes are a new list of rules
they're blessings: a description of who the kingdom belongs to, and an invitation.

games.q: you're on the hillside in Galilee. Jesus sits down and begins to teach. who does he call blessed first?
games.why: blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. the list begins backwards, and keeps going.

practice: Let the eight pass by slowly: the poor in spirit, the meek, the ones who mourn, the ones hungry for justice, the merciful, the clean of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted.
One will catch, maybe because you need mercy, or someone near you does, or a quarrel is waiting for a peacemaker; hold that one for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can ask for that blessing.

wordCard.voice: Beatitudes. From the Latin for blessed and happy: the eight blessings at the start of the Sermon on the Mount, which the Church calls a portrait of Jesus.

orig.note: Greek: blessed, happy, the first word of each Beatitude.
